Series::bessely¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::bessely() const
Series Series::bessely(double order) const

The Singular Cylindrical Solution¶

bessely() evaluates the Bessel function of the second kind, Y_order(x), elementwise. Y_v solves the same cylindrical differential equation as besselj(), but supplies the independent real solution that is singular at the origin. It is used when boundary conditions cannot be represented by J_v alone.

The no-argument form means order zero. bessely(order) applies one finite scalar order to every lane. For positive arguments, integer and non-integer orders are supported. At x=0, order-zero Y tends to negative infinity. On the negative real axis, the real-valued branch is undefined and returns NaN. These are mathematical domain results, not exceptions; an invalid non-finite order is a parameter error and does throw.

Shape and platform are preserved. The result is floating point, with integral input promoted to float64. The transform allocates a result and does not mutate or broadcast its receiver.

Reverse Mode¶

The derivative is evaluated through adjacent orders:

d Y_v(x) / dx = (Y_(v-1)(x) - Y_(v+1)(x)) / 2

Sensitivities inherit the same singularity at zero and the same real-domain restriction on negative arguments.

Examples¶

Example 1. Order zero changes sign between the first two positive samples.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).bessely());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.4445, 0.0883, 0.5104, -0.0169]

Example 2. Supplying order one selects Y_1 rather than changing the shape.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).bessely(1.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.4715, -0.7812, -0.1070, 0.3979]

Example 3. Domain boundaries are represented lane by lane.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0}).bessely());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, -inf, 0.0883]

Example 4. The order-zero reverse result is -Y_1(x).

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.bessely().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.4715, 0.7812, 0.1070]

Example 5. Higher-rank input retains its geometry.

const auto y = pluss::make_series({{0.5, 1.0}, {2.0, 4.0}}).bessely();
std::cout << "dim=" << y.dim()
          << " shape=[" << y.size(0) << "," << y.size(1) << "]\n";

Output¶

dim=2 shape=[2,2]

See Also¶

  • besselj() is finite at the origin for non-negative order.

  • besselk() is the singular but exponentially decaying modified solution.
